title: UK credit history and credit scores for newcomers
summary: Find out what UK credit files contain, how to get free reports, what to do if you cannot register to vote, and how to build a record without taking on unnecessary debt.
content:
# UK credit history and credit scores for newcomers

Evidence checked: 21 November 2026. This guide covers the UK. Voting rules vary by nation and election.

Start with your reports and check that your details are right. Keep the bills you already have up to date. You do not need to borrow or pay interest just to build a credit history.

## Credit history, report and score
Your **credit history** is the record of how you have used credit and paid accounts over time. A **credit report** (or credit file) is the information held by a credit reference agency, such as addresses, reported accounts and payment history, searches and some public records. A **credit score** is a number calculated using a scoring model. The score you see is a guide. There is no single UK score or universal pass mark. Lenders can use their own rules and information you provide. For regulated consumer credit, FCA rules require a proportionate assessment of credit risk and the risk that you cannot afford the repayments. Depending on the application, this can mean looking at income, spending and existing debts. A high consumer score does not guarantee approval or a particular rate. [See evidence](#guide-evidence-basics)

## Why your file may be thin
If you have just moved, UK providers may have little information about your accounts or addresses. A good credit history abroad usually does not transfer automatically. A **thin file** means there is little information on record. If a provider cannot verify you, ask what documents or other evidence it can accept. Give your real address history, including overseas addresses where asked. [See evidence](#guide-evidence-newcomers)

## Get your free credit reports
The three main agencies are **Experian, Equifax and TransUnion**. MoneyHelper also lists **Crediva**. Ask each agency for its **free statutory credit report** through the official links in the evidence below. You can request a report without taking out a paid monitoring subscription or signing up for a trial. The statutory report gives you the file information and may not show the consumer score. Check agencies separately because providers do not always report to all of them. If you cannot verify your identity online or have no file, contact the agency for its alternative process. [See evidence](#guide-evidence-reports)

**Direct links for free reports** — [Experian](https://www.experian.co.uk/consumer/statutory-report.html) · [Equifax](https://www.equifax.co.uk/products/credit/statutory-report) · [TransUnion](https://www.transunion.co.uk/consumer/statutory-credit-report) · [Crediva](https://crediva.co.uk/statutory-credit-report/)

## Check eligibility for the electoral register
Recording your current address on the electoral register can help providers match your identity. Check the Electoral Commission's rules before applying. British, Irish and qualifying Commonwealth citizens living in the UK can generally register if they meet the other conditions. A qualifying Commonwealth citizen normally has permission to enter or stay, or does not need it. In England and Northern Ireland, only certain EU citizens qualify under the EU rules, with the type of election also affecting eligibility. Scotland and Wales have broader rules for their devolved and local elections, including qualifying foreign residents who have permission to enter or stay, or do not need it. Eligibility for those elections does not itself give you a vote in a UK parliamentary election.

If you are eligible, register at your current address and update it when you move. You can opt out of the open register while remaining on the full register used for credit checks, subject to the separate rules for anonymous registration. If you are ineligible, do not register just for credit. Keep your account addresses consistent and ask the lender what other address evidence it accepts. [See evidence](#guide-evidence-voting)

## Build a record with accounts you already need
- **Bills and Direct Debits.** Pay on time and keep enough money in the account before collection day. A Direct Debit is a way to pay. Any credit-file effect depends on whether the provider reports the underlying account and payments. Using a debit card does not itself create a credit repayment record.
- **Mobile contracts.** Some pay-monthly mobile contracts involve a credit check and may report payments or missed payments. Ask what the provider reports, including whether handset finance is separate. Pay-as-you-go is usually a different arrangement and does not normally create a reported repayment history. Choose a plan for your needs and budget.
- **Credit cards.** If you already have one and can afford what you spend, pay on time. Paying the full statement balance by the due date normally avoids interest on ordinary purchases, subject to your card terms. Cash withdrawals can be treated differently. Carrying a balance or paying interest is unnecessary for building a record.
- **Credit-building products and rent reporting.** Check fees, which agencies receive the data, what is reported, and how to cancel. Some services ask for access to bank transaction data through Open Banking. A service can affect one agency's score without helping with the lender you apply to. No product can promise approval or a specific score increase. [See evidence](#guide-evidence-payments)

## Soft searches and hard searches
Using an eligibility checker that confirms it uses a **soft search**, or checking your own report, does not harm your score. A soft check gives an indication, without guaranteeing approval. A formal application usually triggers a **hard search** visible to other lenders. Several in a short period can affect future applications. Check which type of search will be used before agreeing to it. [See evidence](#guide-evidence-searches)

## Fix errors and check how long records stay
Look for wrong names or addresses, incorrect missed payments, old joint financial links and accounts you do not recognise. Save a copy of the relevant entry and send the agency and the organisation that supplied it the details and evidence through their official channels. For suspected identity fraud, contact the provider promptly. Check the other files after the correction. If a data accuracy complaint remains unresolved after raising it with the organisation, you can complain to the ICO. A **Notice of Correction** can add context. It does not erase accurate information or replace a dispute about wrong data. [See evidence](#guide-evidence-disputes)

Missed or late payments can remain visible for up to six years. A default normally stays for six years from the **default date**, even after you repay it. Check that repayment is shown correctly. In England and Wales, a County Court Judgment (CCJ) is usually on the register for six years from the judgment. Full payment within one month can allow removal. If paid later, ask for it to be marked as satisfied. Scotland has decrees and Northern Ireland has its own court procedures. Insolvency entries and restrictions can follow different rules and some remain visible longer. A record disappearing from a report does not by itself cancel any debt. [See evidence](#guide-evidence-retention)

## Newcomer checklist
1. Request the free statutory reports and check your name, addresses, accounts and payment history.
2. Check voter eligibility. If you qualify, register at the address where you live.
3. Set reminders or Direct Debits for bills you can afford, and keep a buffer for payment dates.
4. Correct mistakes before applying. If you need a product, check eligibility with a soft search where available.
